summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct. The prohibition dates from the 2009 penal code, and US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians under that framework, together with arrests and harassment of LGBT people. No source in this inventory identifies any protection, exemption or decriminalisation measure.

The risk posture escalated in December 2023, when President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding "that's what they deserve". Human Rights Watch, reporting in January 2024, condemned the remarks as stoking fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, the Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the speech as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people".

Burundians living under the criminalisation framework responded with terror. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously to SOS Médias Burundi, described the presidential remarks as "a real license to kill (us)". The 2015 State Department report also records that the country's wider political crisis has produced extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns, conditions under which official anti-LGBT rhetoric carries elevated practical risk.
tangentialFactors:
The country's broader human-rights environment is severe. US State Department reporting for 2012 documents torture and extrajudicial executions alongside prolonged pretrial detention, and the 2015 report covers a political crisis marked by extrajudicial killings and arbitrary detention. LGBT people criminalised under the 2009 penal code face this enforcement apparatus rather than a specialised or limited regime.

The January 2024 reporting indicates a shift from statutory prohibition toward open state endorsement of violence. Human Rights Watch framed the president's remarks as stoking fear, and the Iteka League, which operates from exile, described them as an incitement to lynching. The exile status of the principal documented LGBTQ rights body is itself an indicator of the domestic operating space.
localsOnly:
The criminalisation provision applies to Burundian residents as well as visitors, and the 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 State Department reports record discrimination, arrests and harassment affecting gays and lesbians living in the country. Residents report heightened fear following the December 2023 presidential remarks, with members of two domestic LGBTQ associations describing them anonymously as a licence to kill.

Domestic LGBTQ advocacy is largely conducted from outside the country. The Iteka League works in exile and publicly condemned the presidential remarks in January 2024; no source in this inventory records an operating, registered domestic LGBTQ rights organisation.
outOfScopeNotes: The exact penalties attaching to the 2009 criminalisation provision, and whether enforcement has intensified in prosecutions since December 2023, are unresolved: this inventory documents the criminalisation, arrests and harassment, and the presidential remarks, but does not supply sentencing ranges or post-2023 case data. No source addresses gender-marker recognition, legal gender change, screening at entry, asylum treatment of Burundian LGBTQ claimants abroad, or access to gender-affirming care; the dossier makes no claim on these points.
